notes.1: It is important in the study of AS Level Chemistry that candidates are able to describe and explain the important reactions of the elements of the third period of the Periodic Table. In this question there were some good answers to each part. However, many candidates’ answers were marred by the lack of a clear description when it was required.
notes.1a: Most candidates could recall this chemistry correctly; the most common error was describing SiO as amphoteric.
notes.1b: Some candidates gave symbols here instead of names as required in the question.
notes.1c: (i) Most candidates were able to give at least two correct observations. Some, however, described things that were not relevant to the actual experiment such as ‘the solution will turn litmus blue’.
notes.1cii: In this part, the equation was often not balanced, or contained sodium oxide, Na O, as a product.
notes.1d: (i) Many answers to this part were too vague, not specifying a chemical reaction. Examples included ‘car engines’ or ‘factory emissions’.
notes.1e: ‘Reducing agent’ or ‘anti-oxidant’ were well known reasons for the use of SO as a food preservative, while ‘acidic’ was a common incorrect answer.
notes.1f: (i) There were many good diagrams of the arrangement of electrons in the OCS molecule. A common error was to have the O and/or S atoms surrounded by ten electrons.
notes.1fii: A correct ‘dot-and-cross’ diagram was usually followed by the correct bond angle of 180°.
notes.2: The ability to work through a sequence of calculations, such as those in this question, is important in both the theory and the practical parts of AS Level Chemistry. There were many correct answers to this question with candidates demonstrating good mathematical skills in working through the problem. Those candidates who were unable to obtain a correct value for the percentage purity of the ammonium sulfate fertiliser usually used a very unstructured and illogical approach to the calculation.
notes.2a: The majority of candidates gave the correct products, Na SO and H O. Those who offered NaSO 2 4 2 4 or H could not balance the equation.
notes.2b: Those candidates who made an error at an early stage of the calculation but then used their (wrong) answers correctly were given credit.
notes.2i: The equation was well known by the majority of candidates.
notes.2iv: This was less well done with some candidates clearly not understanding the concept of back titration.
notes.2v: Many candidates answered this correctly. Those who used their (wrong) answer to part (iv) correctly were given credit.
notes.2vvi: This was quite well done although some candidates were unable to calculate the M of (NH ) SO r 4 2 4 correctly. Those who used their (wrong) answer to part (v) correctly were given credit.
notes.2vii: There were many candidates who used their answers to preceding parts correctly here.
notes.3: Questions that relate to chemical thermodynamics need to be answered carefully and accurately; Answers must not be ambiguous. While there were many good responses to this question, there were also many candidates who lost credit through a lack of care with equations, definitions or calculations.
notes.3a: Many equations were incorrect because they were unbalanced, lacked or had incorrect state symbols. Definitions of enthalpy change of formation were often insufficiently rigorous and sometimes vague. It was expected that the definition would begin with a phrase such as “the enthalpy change of formation is the enthalpy change when...”. Statements which began “it is when 1 mol of...” were not accepted. Definitions that referred to ‘...the energy required to...’ were not accepted because enthalpy change of formation can be endothermic or exothermic.
notes.3b: (i) Many candidates obtained the correct answer. The main errors seen were having the cycle the wrong way round and getting +49kJmol–1, or using bond energies from the Data Booklet. Candidates were asked to include a sign in their answer; a significant number did not do this and were penalised.
notes.3bii: Candidates usually realised that CO was being used up in the reaction so, as it is a greenhouse gas, global warming would be reduced by the formation of methanol.
notes.3c: Many candidates showed a good understanding of Le Chatelier’s principle in their answers. Only the very best candidates appreciated that with a catalyst the yield does not change because the forward and backward reactions are speeded up by the same amount. Some answers talked about the rate of reaction for which no credit was awarded.
notes.4: Knowledge of the organic chemistry in the AS Level syllabus was generally more secure than in recent years. Many candidates must be congratulated on learning the necessary material very well. However, the presentation of structural, displayed and skeletal formulae still causes problems to many candidates. Information about these different types of formulae is given in Section 10.1 of the syllabus.

notes.5: This question involved application of knowledge of the reactions of functional groups to deduce the identities of some organic compounds. The better candidates solved the problems posed and scored full credit.
notes.5a: This was generally correctly identified, the functional group being carboxylic acid. Examiners did not accept the answer ‘acid’ which was too vague.
notes.5b: (i) Many candidates correctly stated that compound X must be an alcohol. Examiners did not accept ‘hydroxyl’ or ‘−OH’ because these terms could include phenols which do not behave as described in the question.
notes.5bii: Although the question asked candidates to calculate the amount, in moles, of hydrogen atoms, some candidates used the information given about compound X instead.
notes.5iii: The answer that X was oxidised to HOCH CH(OH)CO H was given by many candidates. 2 2

notes.5cii: Many candidates correctly deduced that X was HOCH CH(OH)CHO. Incorrect answers after this stage were given credit in subsequent parts of the question if correct products were given to the reactions mentioned.

notes.general_comments:
This paper tested the candidates’ knowledge and understanding of important aspects of AS Level Chemistry.
The overall standard achieved by candidates was similar to last year, with an encouraging performance in
the calculation questions. Most candidates showed some positive achievement.
Questions 1 and 4 involved much factual recall and showed which candidates had concentrated on this
